questions.enonce_markdown:
10. (a) Trace the events leading to the creation of the League of Nations in 1919.

**(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The League of Nations was an international organisation created by the peace settlement of 1919 to keep peace and settle disputes by discussion; it began its work in January 1920 with its seat in Geneva.

**Events (5 marks, about 1 mark each).**
- **The horror of the First World War (1914-1918).** Millions had died, and many people and leaders wanted to prevent a repeat; the idea of an organisation of nations had been put forward earlier by thinkers and by groups in Britain and the United States.
- **President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 1918).** The fourteenth point called for "a general association of nations" to guarantee the independence and territory of all states.
- **The end of the war,** the armistice of 11 November 1918, and the **Paris Peace Conference (opened January 1919)**, where the Allied leaders, Wilson, Lloyd George and Clemenceau, agreed to set up the League as a first task, although they differed on its powers (France wanted a strong army, Wilson and Britain a weaker body).
- **Drafting the Covenant.** A commission chaired by Wilson drew up the **Covenant** of the League (adopted by the conference in **April 1919**) with Britain's Lord Robert Cecil and General Smuts among its authors.
- **Inclusion in the Treaty of Versailles.** The Covenant became the first part of the Treaty of Versailles, signed on **28 June 1919** and of the other peace treaties; the League came into being when the treaty took effect on **10 January 1920**, even though the United States Senate refused to ratify it.

**Conclusion.** The League was born from the experience of the war, Wilson's ideas and the work of the Paris conference.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) What successes did the League of Nations achieve as regards:

(i) Settlement of international disputes in 1920s

**(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Successes in settling disputes in the 1920s (5 marks).** The League settled several quarrels between smaller states.
- **The Aaland Islands (1921):** a dispute between Sweden and Finland over islands whose people spoke Swedish; the League decided they belonged to **Finland**, with guarantees for the islanders, and both countries accepted.
- **Upper Silesia (1921):** after a plebiscite between Germany and Poland the League divided the industrial area between the two countries, and both accepted the settlement.
- **The Greek-Bulgarian dispute (1925):** after a border incident Greece invaded Bulgaria; the League ordered both to withdraw, and Greece obeyed and paid compensation.
- **Other cases:** disputes over the Memel territory, the Mosul question between Turkey and Britain (Iraq) and the quarrel between Poland and Lithuania were handled by discussions, and the League also organised the **Saar** administration until the plebiscite of 1935.
- **Reasons for success:** the states concerned were small or wished to avoid war, and the powers (Britain and France) supported the League in this period.

(Failures such as **Corfu (1923)**, where Italy ignored the League, and **Vilna**, show that the League could not always enforce its decisions.)

**Successes in humanitarian work (5 marks).**
- **Refugees and prisoners of war.** Under the High Commissioner **Fridtjof Nansen**, the League helped to send home hundreds of thousands of prisoners of war after the First World War, and issued the **Nansen passport** (1922) to stateless refugees.
- **The International Labour Organisation (ILO)** worked for better working conditions, hours and wages in the member countries.
- **The Health Organisation** fought epidemics such as typhus and malaria and spread medical knowledge.
- **Fight against slavery and forced labour:** the League's Slavery Commission prepared the **Slavery Convention of 1926** and pressed states such as Ethiopia and Liberia to end slavery.
- **Control of drugs** (opium) and the protection of women and children against trafficking.
- **The Mandates Commission** supervised the territories taken from Germany and Turkey, receiving reports (and petitions), including the Cameroons.
- **The Permanent Court of International Justice** (1921) and the **Committee for Intellectual Cooperation** helped to spread law and learning.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Why did the League of Nations fail in the1930s?

**(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Reasons for failure (5 marks, about 1 mark each).**
- **Absence of important members.** The **USA never joined**; Germany joined in 1926 but left in 1933, Japan left in 1933 and Italy in 1937, and the USSR was a member only from 1934 (and was expelled in 1939), so the League was not truly universal.
- **No army of its own.** The League depended on members' troops and on **economic sanctions**, which were weak and not applied by all.
- **Selfishness of Britain and France.** They were its leading members but cared first for their own interests and the fear of another war; they did not wish to risk war for faraway countries.
- **Failure over Manchuria (1931-1933).** When Japan invaded Manchuria the League sent the **Lytton Commission**, condemned Japan (1933) but did nothing; Japan simply left.
- **Failure over Abyssinia (1935-1936).** Italy invaded Ethiopia; the sanctions did not include oil and were lifted, and the **Hoare-Laval Pact** showed that Britain and France were ready to reward the aggressor.
- **The Great Depression** made countries concentrate on their own problems and encouraged aggressive nationalism.
- **The rule of unanimity** in the Council and the Assembly made decisions slow and difficult.
- **Failure of disarmament** (Disarmament Conference 1932-1934) and the later aggression of Hitler (Rhineland 1936, Austria 1938, Czechoslovakia 1939), which the League did not stop; the Second World War began in 1939.

**Conclusion.** Lacking power, the support of the USA and the will of Britain and France, the League could not stop aggressors in the 1930s and was replaced by the United Nations in 1945-1946.
